title: Attacking the castled king

D0.outcome: Explains that a castled king's defence is its pawn cover and the pieces near it, and that an attack needs attackers to match the defenders.

D1.outcome: Counts the attackers who can reach and the defenders who can answer around a castled king, and names the weakened squares.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, chooses among bringing one more piece (opening a file), exchanging a defender, or not attacking, and recognises when the pawn cover has been loosened.

D3.outcome: Predicts how a defender's bishop or knight covering the holes refutes the attack, and checks the declined lines.

misconceptions: A sacrifice near the king always works.
Counting attackers is enough; the quality of the defenders does not matter.
conditions: In a king attack the number of attackers needed is compared with the defenders available; with exactly enough on both sides, moving any defender tips the balance.
The weak point is the pawn cover in front of the king, as after the king's knight pawn has advanced a square.
contrasts: The same pawn move, but a defender piece covers the key squares.
Counting defenders without checking which can really be removed.
A queenside pawn move that does not affect the king.

soft_prereq_notes.TAC.BACKRANK.D2: the back-rank weakness is the simplest castled-king attack

title: Attacking a king in the centre

D0.outcome: Explains why a king that has not castled becomes a target when lines open, and what an attacker needs (open lines, a lead in development).

D1.outcome: Told to attack the king in the centre, finds the line-opening move (pawn break or sacrifice) and the follow-up.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, decides whether to open the centre or keep it closed, punishes an uncastled king when ahead in development, and refrains when behind.

D3.outcome: Counts the pieces that can join and tests the declined lines; predicts that castling or an interposition ends the attack.

misconceptions: Sacrifice whenever the king is exposed.
Never sacrifice.
sources: sources/sheets/znosko-borovsky_middle-game.md §4 C33 (king in the centre: target the pawn that shelters him, stop castling, open files)
conditions: The opponent is behind in development and cannot castle, or lines can be opened quickly, and several attacking pieces are in play.
Keep the option of castling rather than committing early, unless the opponent's central plan is known; open centre lines punish the uncastled king.
contrasts: The same sacrifice when the opponent has castled and developed.
A sacrifice from the Max Lange attack that no master defended after a novelty reopened it (judged by results, not analysis).
A closed centre.

soft_prereq_notes.FND.CASTLE.D1: the uncastled king is the target

title: Committing to a direct attack

D0.outcome: Explains that a direct attack, once started, needs every available piece and certainty, and that stopping halfway can be worse than not starting.

D1.outcome: Counts the pieces available and decides whether every piece can be brought in.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, decides to continue, break off or accept a repetition, and avoids starting without enough force.

D3.outcome: Tests whether breaking off or repeating is better than pressing on, and predicts which piece, coming in last, decides.

misconceptions: Never break off a direct attack.
Start an attack because the king looks weak.
conditions: Enough force to be sure; every available piece is brought in, and the last piece often decides.
The simple winning move may be preferable until experience allows the complication.
contrasts: 'never break off' is absolute; engines often show that regrouping or a repetition is better.
Starting an attack because the king looks weak, without counting the pieces.
A position where the simple winning move exists.

title: The bishop sacrifice on h7 (Greek gift)

D0.outcome: States the conditions for the sacrifice on h7 (the knight can reach g5, the queen can reach h5, the bishop is on the diagonal, no defending knight or bishop covers) and what the sacrifice is for.

D1.outcome: When told 'Greek gift', finds Bxh7+ and the follow-up, and names the conditions that hold.

D2.outcome: In a mixed set, plays it only where the conditions hold, declines where a defender covers h7 or h5 or the king escapes, and recognises the declined line.

D3.outcome: Calculates the declined lines and predicts which single defender (knight on f6, a covering bishop) kills it.

misconceptions: The sacrifice on h7 always works.
The sacrifice works whenever the bishop is on the diagonal.
sources: sources/sheets/capablanca_chess-fundamentals.md §4 CI-27, CI-29; §8 item 13 (conditions are ours; verify by engine)
conditions: The sacrifice is supported by two pieces.
Verified at the wins-or-mates level, never as an unqualified correct answer; practical versus sound is labelled.
contrasts: The same sacrifice with a defender piece covering h7 or h5.
The greedy 'famous sacrifice' where the declined line refutes it; every attack family needs such items.
Queenside pawn moves.

title: Pace of the attack

D0.outcome: Explains that the speed of an attack follows the margin of superiority and whether the enemy's reserves can arrive.

D1.outcome: Told a position, says 'quick' or 'moderate' and gives the reason (king in the centre; sound pawn cover).

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, chooses between forcing play and methodical strengthening of strong points, and does not mistake a slow plan for passivity.

D3.outcome: Predicts how the arrival of one reserve piece changes the right pace.

misconceptions: Every attack must be fast.
A slow plan is passive.
conditions: Large superiority in an area with real weaknesses calls for quick, forcing play; unclear superiority calls for a moderate pace.
The criterion 'clearly defined' is not operationalised in the source.
contrasts: A slow plan against a king that can still castle, giving the opponent time.
Forcing play against a sound castled position with no weakness.
A position where defender's reserves are already in place.

soft_prereq_notes.CAL.TREE.D1: pace is chosen by counting the lines

title: Pawn storms and opposite-side castling

D0.outcome: Explains that a pawn storm needs pieces massed behind it and a pawn barrier that can be broken, and that with opposite-side castling the game becomes a race.

D1.outcome: Finds the lever that opens a file against the castled king and counts the pieces behind it.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, decides whether to storm, defend or counter, and labels the choice practical or sound.

D3.outcome: Predicts when the storm fails (intact barrier, defender's pieces near) and counts the race.

misconceptions: Always storm the king.
Pawn moves are free when attacking.
conditions: Many pieces can be massed behind the pawns before the opponent counterattacks the advanced pawns.
With opposite castling, pawns are cheap and open lines are the point; speed decides.
Against a castled king the pawn attack succeeds only if the pawn barrier on the third rank can be broken.
contrasts: The same pawn moves, with the barrier intact and the defender's pieces near.
'the player who attacks first usually wins' is folk wisdom, not a theorem.
Play on the opposite wing.
note: Label practical vs sound (CD-5).

title: Tangible superiority before attacking

D0.outcome: Explains that an attack needs a tangible superiority at the point of attack (in working force or reach), and that without it the counter-attack finds the attacker disordered.

D1.outcome: In a middlegame position, counts the attacking pieces that bear on the target area against the defenders and says 'attack now', 'not yet' or 'no'.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, chooses among attacking, finishing development and defending, and punishes a premature attack by the opponent.

D3.outcome: Predicts how a one-feature change (the opponent has castled and developed; the centre is closed) removes the licence to attack, and why a development deficit voids a tempting sacrifice.

D4.outcome: In own games, records the superiority count before attacking decisions, and the review compares it with the result.

misconceptions: Whoever has the initiative should attack.
Attack because it is my move.
An exposed king always justifies a sacrifice.
conditions: Attack when better developed, with more force aimed at the weak area and a concrete target.
A development lead licenses direct attack and can justify sacrifices to open lines; a development deficit voids it.
A very good opponent rarely offers the conditions for a quick attack.
contrasts: An attack on a fully developed opponent with no weak target (a premature attack that runs out of steam).
The same sacrifice when the opponent has castled and developed.
A closed centre or a quiet endgame-like position.

title: Entering variations without the pieces

D0.outcome: Explains why the variation is entered in the head and checked on the board only at the end.

D1.outcome: Enters a six-ply variation without moving pieces, then states the position and the key threat in it, in at least 7 of 10 tests.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, finds a refutation 8 plies deep that needs a quiet move in the middle, with no board manipulation.

D3.outcome: Holds two branches of a tree at once and compares their end positions without writing them down.

misconceptions: Moving pieces on the board while thinking is the same skill.
Blind calculation needs a photographic memory.
sources: docs/curriculum-map-v1.md §2 S4 (Kotov, Aagaard, Ramesh, Dvoretsky, Rowson, Heisman, all [R] in the map) (CAL.BLIND T5-6)
conditions: The learner can already visualise five-ply lines reliably (CAL.VISUALIZE D3).
contrasts: The line is held until the first quiet move, then confused with an earlier position.
Holding too many branches and mixing their end positions.
A position that needs only a one-move check.

title: Candidate moves: list and prune

D0.outcome: Explains why moves are listed before they are analysed and why a candidate is dropped only for a concrete reason.

D1.outcome: Writes a list of two to four candidates for a given position, starting with the forcing moves and including one quiet move, each with a one-line purpose.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, produces a list that contains the best move in at least 8 of 10, with no more than four moves.

D3.outcome: Prunes a list to one move by naming a concrete refutation for each dropped candidate, and notices when a new candidate appears only after the first move is played.

misconceptions: The first move that comes to mind is the candidate and the rest is padding.
A move is dropped because it looks bad, not because a refutation was found.
sources: docs/curriculum-map-v1.md §2 S4 (Kotov, Aagaard, Ramesh, Dvoretsky, Rowson, Heisman, all [R] in the map)
docs/council-synthesis.md Round 3 and CD-3 (candidate lists, analysis tree)
sources/sheets/emlasker_common-sense.md §4.11 (three kinds of move) and §4.13 (plans rather than trees)
conditions: Not a forced position; more than one plan is plausible.
Forcing moves are listed first; quiet moves are included because positional moves are neither threats nor parries.
contrasts: A list of near-duplicates (the same idea in two move orders).
Dropping a candidate by feel and later finding it was the only move.
A forced reply to a check, where there is nothing to list.

soft_prereq_notes.TAC.NONE.D1: 'nothing forcing' is a legitimate result of the search

title: Comparing resulting positions

D0.outcome: Explains that candidates are compared by the positions they lead to, and that a count of moves or material is only the first step.

D1.outcome: Given two or three resulting positions, ranks them and names the deciding feature of each (activity, structure, king safety, material).

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, chooses the better resulting position when the difference is positional rather than material, in at least 7 of 10.

D3.outcome: States which feature decides the comparison and predicts how a one-feature change reverses it; spots a fictitious gain that the count rewards.

misconceptions: More pieces developed or more advanced means better.
If the line wins a pawn, the resulting position is better.
sources: docs/curriculum-map-v1.md §2 S4 (Kotov, Aagaard, Ramesh, Dvoretsky, Rowson, Heisman, all [R] in the map)
sources/sheets/znosko-borovsky_middle-game.md §4 C02-C07, §5 items 10, 12 (formal count, audit, difference; counts that mislead)
conditions: Reliable only when the formal counts agree and nothing tactical is hanging.
The check on each extra move is what it was used for, and where the pieces are.
contrasts: Ahead on every count and lost to one concrete idea.
The same move count with moves wasted on rim-pawn pushes.
Both continuations transpose into the same position.

soft_prereq_notes.POS.GOODBAD.D2: piece quality is part of the comparison

title: The opponent's best resource

D0.outcome: Explains that analysis is not finished until the opponent has had his best reply, including quiet and defensive moves.

D1.outcome: For a given line, lists the opponent's check, capture, threat and best defensive move at each step.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, finds the refutation when the first-choice line has a hidden defensive resource, and accepts the line when none exists.

D3.outcome: In positions where several natural defences look alike, tests each and finds the only move that holds; predicts how a small change makes a second defence work.

misconceptions: If I can't see a defence, there is none.
The opponent will play the move my line expects.
sources: docs/curriculum-map-v1.md §2 S4 (Kotov, Aagaard, Ramesh, Dvoretsky, Rowson, Heisman, all [R] in the map)
docs/council-synthesis.md Round 3 (Dvoretsky: look for the opponent's best resource)
sources/sheets/emlasker_common-sense.md §4.16 (find the only defence; do not trust an unverified perpetual)
conditions: Applies to every line chosen for a critical decision.
Several natural defences look similar and only one holds.
contrasts: A combination judged unsound without noticing the quiet follow-up that makes it work (the champion's own game).
Assuming the opponent's reply is the one the line needs.
Forced mate lines where all defences are enumerated.

soft_prereq_notes.TAC.ZWISCHENZUG.D1: the opponent's in-between moves are part of his best resource

title: How deep, and when to stop

D0.outcome: Explains that depth is a resource: spend it where the decision is critical, forcing or irreversible, and stop when more depth cannot change the choice.

D1.outcome: For a position, says which line deserves the deepest check and gives the reason; says which lines can be left shallow.

D2.outcome: On a set of positions with a stated time budget, spends more time on critical positions and less on routine ones, as the time log shows.

D3.outcome: Names the stopping point of a long variation with a reason (quiet position reached, evaluation stable, forced win found) and revisits it only if the reason changes.

misconceptions: Thinking longer always improves the move.
A stopping point is arbitrary.
sources: docs/curriculum-map-v1.md §2 S4 (Kotov, Aagaard, Ramesh, Dvoretsky, Rowson, Heisman, all [R] in the map)
docs/council-synthesis.md Round 3 (the skill is allocating depth; no printed method trains it)
conditions: The position has a critical decision and a time budget.
Stopping is justified by a stable evaluation or a forced result, not by tiredness.
contrasts: A deep think on a move with an obvious only-reply.
A quick move in a critical position because the first idea 'looks right'.
A position in the opening book, where depth is replaced by recall.

soft_prereq_notes.PRA.PRESSURE.D1: time pressure limits the depth that is available

title: Long lines and accuracy under fatigue

D0.outcome: Explains why accuracy falls in a long game and what routine slows the fall.

D1.outcome: Calculates a ten-ply line at the end of a long training session with no more errors than in the fresh baseline.

D2.outcome: In a two-hour set of positions, keeps the rate of blunders flat across the second half, as the log shows.

D3.outcome: Names a personal fatigue marker and the routine that corrects it, and the log confirms it works over several sessions.

misconceptions: Fatigue only affects speed, not accuracy.
sources: docs/curriculum-map-v1.md §2 S4 (Kotov, Aagaard, Ramesh, Dvoretsky, Rowson, Heisman, all [R] in the map) (CAL.ENDURANCE T6-7)
conditions: Session length is long enough to show a fall in accuracy.
contrasts: The first-hour accuracy figure is used as the standard for the third hour.
Practising long lines only when fresh, then meeting them tired in tournaments.
A ten-minute quiz.
note: Few sources in the sheets; mainly from the map's S4 and S10 descriptions.

title: The analysis tree

D0.outcome: Explains the analysis tree: each branch is examined once, its end-verdict noted, and only then is a move chosen.

D1.outcome: Draws a tree for three candidates with two replies each to four plies and gives a one-word verdict at each end.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, builds the tree without revisiting the same branch, and reaches the same verdict as the engine check on at least 7 of 10 positions.

D3.outcome: In positions with many forcing replies, prunes by forcing moves first, notes transpositions, and records the result so a branch is not recomputed.

misconceptions: Jumping between branches is a sign of thoroughness (it is the usual cause of missed lines).
A deeper tree is a better tree.
sources: docs/curriculum-map-v1.md §2 S4 (Kotov, Aagaard, Ramesh, Dvoretsky, Rowson, Heisman, all [R] in the map)
docs/council-synthesis.md Round 3 (Kotov: each branch once; Aagaard: avoid repeated rechecking)
sources/sheets/emlasker_common-sense.md §4.13 (analysis by plans, not trees; completeness claims suspect)
conditions: Used when the position is concrete enough that branches end in a clear verdict within about four plies.
Plan enumeration works when the number of strategic plans is small, but a claim that no other plan exists is rarely provable.
contrasts: Rechecking the same branch in the same order (thinking inertia).
Declaring that the enumerated plans are all the plans, and missing an extra resource.
A quiet position where branches never end in a verdict.

title: Visualising a line

D0.outcome: Explains why calculation means tracking the pieces and attacked squares, not a mental picture of the board.

D1.outcome: For a named candidate, states the position after the next two plies and which piece is then attacked, with the board visible but no pieces moved.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, decides whether a three-ply line loses a piece (including an uncovered attack) without moving pieces, in at least 7 of 10.

D3.outcome: Holds a five-ply forcing line with a capture and a check, then lists the legal replies and the attacked pieces at the end of it.

D4.outcome: In own games, writes down the position after the intended line and the expected reply for chosen moves, and the record matches the game in at least 8 of 10.

misconceptions: Visualising is seeing a clear picture; it is better built by tracking what moved and what is now attacked.
A longer line is better; accuracy past the first capture matters more than length.
sources: docs/curriculum-map-v1.md §2 S4 (Kotov, Aagaard, Ramesh, Dvoretsky, Rowson, Heisman, all [R] in the map)
sources/sheets/capablanca_chess-fundamentals.md §4 CI-17 (d) (calculation by visualising future positions is what counts)
conditions: Lines are short and the learner re-anchors on attacked pieces after each move.
Captures and discovered attacks are the points where tracking fails.
contrasts: Forgetting which piece a capture removed, so the final position is wrong.
A knight route miscounted by one move (opposite corners need six).
A one-move tactic that needs no line tracking.

soft_prereq_notes.FND.PIECE.KNIGHT.D1: knight routes are the hardest to track

title: Counter-attack

D0.outcome: Explains that a counter-attack works only if your own defence is complete and your threats arrive first.

D1.outcome: Counts both sides' move requirements and says 'counter-attack' or 'defend'.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, picks the moment to switch from defence to attack and avoids the half-hearted third option.

D3.outcome: Predicts how one tempo or a bare king reverses a counter-attack, and what material it costs.

misconceptions: The best defence is always attack.
conditions: Your own defence is complete and the opponent's position has weak points or pieces that allow uninterrupted threats.
Switching from passive to active comes when the opponent tries to demolish the whole defensive system.
contrasts: The attack is one move slower, or leaves the king bare.
Neither defending nor attacking decisively (the half-hearted third option).
A purely defensive endgame.

title: Diagnosing a worse position

D0.outcome: States the defender's four questions: what is my chief weakness, what is the opponent's chief threat, is his advantage enough to win, will it decide in the middlegame or in the ending.

D1.outcome: For a defender's position, writes the chief weakness and the chief threat in one sentence each.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, picks the move that addresses both the weakness and the threat, with a long plan rather than one parry at a time.

D3.outcome: When material must be lost, decides which and for what ending.

misconceptions: Defending means making only direct parries.
When badly worse, resign (dated advice).
sources: docs/curriculum-map-v1.1.md §3 (DEF.DIAGNOSE: replace the passive doctrine with active defence)
conditions: The opponent's lead is real but not crushing.
Defend with a long plan; the aim is to restore your own freedom of choice.
contrasts: Parrying each threat in turn without a plan.
Following the advice to give up when hopelessly worse.
An overwhelming disadvantage where the question is swindle chances rather than diagnosis.

title: Fortresses in the middlegame and ending

D0.outcome: Explains a fortress as a set-up the stronger side cannot break although it is ahead in material.

D1.outcome: Told a material imbalance, builds the fortress set-up and names the squares that must stay covered.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, decides whether to aim for a fortress, and spots an enemy fortress he cannot break.

D3.outcome: Tests a claimed fortress by naming the break that would defeat it and showing it does not work.

misconceptions: More material always wins.
conditions: The stronger side has no entry square or breakthrough and the weaker side has a safe waiting move.
contrasts: The set-up has one entry square left uncovered.
The stronger side can force a zugzwang against the set-up.
A position where an exchange sacrifice breaks the set-up trivially.

soft_prereq_notes.PRA.RESIST.D2: the practical side of building a fortress in a worse position

note: Defined with END.FORTRESS (T5); middlegame fortresses are rarer and need engine verification.

title: A defender's resources

D0.outcome: Explains that a defender has several resources (move, protect, block, capture, counter-threat, vacate-then-support, return material).

D1.outcome: Given an attack, lists the defender's resources and picks the one that meets the chief threat.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, defends correctly where the threat is real and does not over-defend where it is not; vacates a weak point before supporting it.

D3.outcome: Finds the only defence among several similar moves and verifies a claimed perpetual.

misconceptions: Defence is passive.
conditions: When really compromised, find the weak points, vacate them if they hold important pieces, then support them from squares that are hard to reach.
Defence engages the opponent's reserves with the rest of the army.
contrasts: Supporting a weak point while the important piece is still on it.
'follow the rules and you will find a defence however dangerous the attack looks' is over-promising.
The important piece is not on the target square.

title: Pawn cover in front of the king

D0.outcome: Explains the pawn cover in front of a castled king and that a pawn push loosens it.

D1.outcome: For a given castled position and a pawn move, names the squares the move weakens and the enemy pieces that can use them.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, tells dangerous pawn moves from harmless ones near the king.

D3.outcome: Predicts how a defender's piece (a bishop on g2, a knight) covering the weakened squares changes the verdict.

misconceptions: Every pawn move near the king is a weakness.
conditions: The king is castled on that side and the opponent's queen, rook and knight can reach the weakened squares.
contrasts: The same pawn move, but a defender piece covers the key squares.
'every pawn move near the king is a weakness'.
A queenside pawn move.

title: Defensive exchanges

D0.outcome: Explains that a defender trades the attacker's best pieces and relieves a cramp by exchanging.

D1.outcome: Given an attack, picks the trade that removes its most dangerous piece.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, chooses between trading, counter-attacking and holding, and avoids trades that remove his own defenders.

D3.outcome: Predicts which trade leaves the king bare and which kills the attack.

misconceptions: Any trade eases the defence.
sources: sources/sheets/capablanca_chess-fundamentals.md §4 CI-42 (fewer pieces help the cramped side)
conditions: The trade removes an attacker that cannot be replaced, and does not strip a defender.
contrasts: A trade that removes the last defender near the king.
A trade that frees the attacker's remaining pieces.
A trade that changes nothing about the attack.
note: Few sheet sources; conditions mainly from CAP CI-42 and EML 4.15.

title: Defence by waiting

D0.outcome: Explains defence by economy: do not change your own position voluntarily, skip superfluous defensive moves, and wait until the opponent has spent time on his threat.

D1.outcome: In a position where the opponent's move looks like a threat, decides whether it is real and plays a useful move when it is not.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled sets rich in no-threat positions, plays correctly without pushing a rook pawn to stop a pin or chasing a well-placed knight with a knight pawn.

D3.outcome: States when waiting fails (a plan, once begun, cannot be stopped later) and contrasts it with prophylaxis.

misconceptions: Every pawn move to meet a possible threat is wise.
Passive defence loses.
sources: docs/curriculum-map-v1.1.md §3 (DEF.WAIT T4; a source of no-threat items)
conditions: Applies when the position is equal or better and there is no real target.
Superfluous defensive moves (preventing something that is no threat) spoil many games.
contrasts: The same-looking move that is a genuine threat needing prevention.
Ignoring the opponent's preparations contradicts prophylactic thought where a plan, once begun, cannot be stopped.
A position with nothing to defend.

title: Pawn breakthrough

D0.outcome: Explains the breakthrough: sacrificing a pawn or two to create a passed pawn when several pawns face each other.

D1.outcome: Finds the breakthrough move in a 3-against-3 pawn skeleton when it exists.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled pawn endings, tells when a breakthrough wins, draws or loses, depending on who is nearer to queening and who has the move.

D3.outcome: Verifies the breakthrough by counting and predicts how one extra tempo for the defender changes the result.

misconceptions: The breakthrough always works if there are more pawns.
sources: docs/curriculum-map-v1.md §2 S7 (Chesscademy 'Opposition and Breakthrough', title only)
conditions: The attacker's pawns are further advanced; with the other side to move the same position is drawn.
contrasts: The same skeleton with the wrong side to move.
Believing the breakthrough always works.
Pawns not in contact.

soft_prereq_notes.END.KPK.D1: the resulting passed pawn is a K+P problem

title: Fortresses in endings

D0.outcome: Explains a fortress as a set-up the stronger side cannot break despite its extra material.

D1.outcome: Told a material imbalance, builds the fortress and names the squares that must stay covered.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled endings, decides whether to aim for a fortress and spots one that cannot be broken.

D3.outcome: Tests a claimed fortress by naming the break and showing it fails, using the tablebase where possible.

misconceptions: More material always wins.
conditions: Wrong-coloured bishop with a rook pawn: the defender's king reaching the corner holds the draw.
The stronger side has no entry square or breakthrough, and the weaker side keeps a safe waiting move.
condition_sources: CAP CI-14 (c); EDL K27 (b); MAP11 §4 verified
contrasts: One entry square is left uncovered.
The stronger side can force a zugzwang against the set-up.
A trivial exchange sacrifice that wins at once.

soft_prereq_notes.END.QUEEN-PAWN.D1: stalemate fortresses are often built against the queen

title: Key squares

D0.outcome: Explains key squares: if the attacking king reaches one, the pawn queens whoever is to move.

D1.outcome: Given a pawn on a rank, marks its key squares.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled K+P positions, predicts the result with the key-square rule, including the rook-pawn exception and who is to move.

D3.outcome: Compares the key-square and opposition methods on the same position, and explains why the sixth-rank rule is a special case.

misconceptions: King directly in front of the pawn means it cannot be won (a rule of thumb).
sources: sources/sheets/capablanca_chess-fundamentals.md §7 row 6 (replace the rule of thumb with key squares)
conditions: Key squares as the primary rule; the sixth-rank threshold is a special case.
contrasts: The 'king directly in front means no win' rule of thumb treated as exact.
The sixth-rank opposition rule misses cases the key-square rule handles.
A position with additional pieces, where key squares alone do not decide.

title: The king as a fighting piece

D0.outcome: Explains that in endings the king becomes a fighting piece that should head for the centre or the targets, unlike in the middlegame.

D1.outcome: Told to bring the king, routes it to the centre or to a passed pawn in the fewest moves in a simple ending.

D2.outcome: In mixed positions, decides whether to centralise the king: centralises when queens are off and no mating threats exist, keeps it home when heavy pieces and checks remain.

D3.outcome: Counts a king-against-passed-pawn race and predicts the effect of a bishop or rook check that punishes a hasty king move.

misconceptions: A king in the centre is always dangerous.
Keep the king at home in an ending.
sources: docs/curriculum-map-v1.1.md §3 (END.KING-ACTIVE, merged from Cap, Nimz, EmL)
conditions: Queens (and most pieces) are off and there are no immediate mating threats against the king.
Centralise the king as soon as the endgame begins, for activity and to limit the enemy king's squares.
contrasts: Queens are still on and a rook lift is available to the opponent.

conditions: The knight jumps two squares along a rank or file and one at a right angle; pieces in between do not matter.
It cannot land on its own piece but may take an enemy piece.
contrasts: On the edge or in a corner the knight has fewer than eight landing squares.
Pieces standing next to the knight do not block it.

title: How the pawn moves

D0.outcome: Says that a pawn moves straight forward, never backward, captures one square diagonally forward, and may move two squares on its first move.

D1.outcome: When told 'pawn', marks every square a pawn can move to: forward onto empty squares only, diagonally forward only to capture.

D2.outcome: In a busy position where the piece is not named, marks every square the pawn can move to, including a blocked pawn and one on its starting rank.

D3.outcome: Says in how many moves a pawn can reach a given square, counting captures that change its file.

misconceptions: The pawn captures straight ahead.
A pawn can always move two squares.
A pawn can move backward or sideways.
A pawn may move diagonally onto an empty square.
conditions: A pawn moves straight forward onto an empty square (two squares from its starting rank if both are empty).
It captures one square diagonally forward, only onto an enemy piece; a piece directly in front blocks it and cannot be captured.
contrasts: A pawn facing an enemy piece directly ahead cannot move forward and cannot take it, but it may still capture diagonally.
An enemy piece two squares ahead does not stop a pawn from making its one-square move.

title: How the queen moves

D0.outcome: Says that the queen moves like a rook and a bishop together.

D1.outcome: When told 'queen', marks every square the queen can move to, stopping in front of its own pieces and at the first enemy piece on each line.

D2.outcome: In a busy position where the piece is not named, marks every square the queen can reach.

D3.outcome: Without a board, says whether the queen reaches a square in one move or needs two, and names a square from which it attacks two lines at once.

misconceptions: The queen can also move like a knight.
Because it is the strongest piece, the queen can safely take anything.
conditions: The queen has the moves of a rook and a bishop from the same square.
Each of its eight lines is blocked separately: a blocker on one line does not affect the others.
contrasts: The queen does not jump like a knight.
A piece blocking the rank does not stop the queen using the file and the diagonals.

title: How the rook moves

D0.outcome: Says that a rook slides any distance along a rank or file and cannot jump over pieces.

D1.outcome: When told 'rook', marks every square a rook can move to: it stops in front of its own pieces and may take the first enemy piece in its way.

D2.outcome: In a busy position where the piece is not named, marks every square the piece on a given square can reach.

D3.outcome: Without a board, says whether a rook can reach a far square in one move, and if not in how many, and notices when one blocker is all that stops it.

misconceptions: The rook can jump over pieces.
The rook can land on a square held by its own piece.
The rook cannot capture a piece standing in its way.
conditions: The rook moves along a rank or a file for any number of free squares.
It stops in front of its own piece and may take the first enemy piece on its line, and then stops there.
contrasts: A piece on the line blocks everything behind it: the squares behind it cannot be reached in one move.
Pieces that stand off the rook's rank and file do not change where the rook can go.

title: Promotion

D0.outcome: Says that a pawn reaching the last rank must become a queen, rook, bishop or knight, never a king or a pawn.

D1.outcome: Promotes a pawn to a queen when told, and capture-promotes when straight ahead is blocked.

D2.outcome: Decides whether a pawn can promote on this move, straight ahead or by capture.

D3.outcome: Chooses a promotion other than the queen when the queen would stalemate in a won ending, or when another piece gives checkmate.

misconceptions: A pawn must always become a queen.
You can only promote to a piece you have lost.
A pawn can become a king.
conditions: A pawn reaching the last rank becomes a queen, rook, bishop or knight at once, as part of the move.
The queen is usually best, but check whether the promotion gives stalemate or whether another piece gives checkmate.
contrasts: Promoting to a queen can stalemate the enemy king where a rook would win.
The pieces you already have do not limit what you may promote to.

title: Which special move applies
origin: foundation worker (combiner node added after a lesson and items asked for a mixed special-move check)

D0.outcome: Names the three special moves (castling, en passant, promotion) and what makes each one possible.

D1.outcome: Told which special move to look for, finds it in a position.

D2.outcome: In mixed positions where nobody names the move, says which special move (if any) is available to the side to move.

misconceptions: A special move is always available when the pieces are in place.
Only one kind of special move can ever be on the board.
sources: docs/curriculum-map-v1.md §2 S1 (FND.SPECIAL split into castle/en passant/promote; this node is the mixed 'which one?' check added by the foundation worker)
conditions: Each special move has its own condition: castling needs unmoved king and rook with a clear, unattacked path; en passant needs a two-square advance on the previous move; promotion needs a pawn on the last rank.
A position can offer none of them, and the correct answer is then 'none'.
contrasts: A position that looks like en passant but the double-step happened two moves ago.
The rest of the pieces, for deciding which special move is legal.

title: Stalemate

D0.outcome: Says that stalemate is a draw: the side to move is not in check but has no legal move.

D1.outcome: Tells checkmate from stalemate when told it is one of the two.

D2.outcome: In mixed positions names check, checkmate, stalemate or ongoing, and notices before moving when its own move would stalemate the enemy.

D3.outcome: In a won ending chooses the move that wins instead of stalemating, and knows that stalemate can save a lost game.

misconceptions: Stalemate is a win for the side that moved last.
Stalemate is the same as checkmate.
Having a big material lead means stalemate cannot happen.
conditions: Stalemate: the side to move is not in check and has no legal move; the game is drawn.
Before a move that boxes the king in, count the legal moves it has left.
contrasts: Same material, one move different: the king is attacked (mate, a win) or not attacked (stalemate, a draw).
How much extra material the stronger side has does not prevent stalemate.

title: Piece values

D0.outcome: Says the usual point values: pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9; the king is never traded.

D1.outcome: Given two pieces, says which is worth more and by how much, and adds up the material on each side.

D2.outcome: Judges a trade, for example a rook for a bishop and a pawn, as winning, equal or losing material without the values shown.

D3.outcome: Gives a position where a piece is worth more or less than its usual points and says why, treating the values as a guide and not a law.

misconceptions: The point values are exact laws, the same in every position.
Counting pieces instead of their values.
conditions: Pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5 and queen 9 are a rule of thumb for comparing trades.
A trade is good when you receive more points than you give.
contrasts: Giving a rook for a bishop and a pawn is 5 for 4 and loses a point although three pieces change hands.
The colour of the pieces does not change their values.

title: Board vision without the board

D0.outcome: Explains why a position can be held in mind as a list of pieces and the squares they attack, and gives one task that exercises it.

D1.outcome: With the board hidden, names the colour of a given square, the squares a knight on it reaches in one and two moves, and the squares on a named diagonal.

D2.outcome: From a piece list and three moves in notation with no board, says where each piece stands and which of them is attacked at the end.

D3.outcome: Holds a six-ply line containing a capture, a check and a pawn move, then answers questions about the final position (what is attacked; the legal replies to the check) with no board.

D4.outcome: Over ten games, states the resulting position after his intended move and the likely reply before playing for chosen moves, and is right on the attacked pieces in at least 8 of 10 checks.

misconceptions: Visualising means seeing a picture of the board; it works better as tracking pieces and attacked squares.
Distance in knight moves is easy to count (a knight needs six moves between opposite corners, five is a common slip).
sources: docs/chesscademy-research.md (Visualizing Pieces lesson title, per MAP1 §2 S2)

title: Developing and time-wasting moves

D1.outcome: In an early opening position, picks the move that develops with most effect and names a move that wastes time (a rook-pawn move, a needless queen move).

D3.outcome: Predicts how the position's character (a settled structure, a pinned knight) makes a quiet or non-developing move right, and which default it overrides.

misconceptions: Knights before bishops is a law.
Develop fast means make as many different piece moves as possible.
Never move a pawn beyond the centre pawns.

contrasts: A useful-looking rook-pawn move adds no force while the opponent has an open line to a weak point.

A real pin where a rook-pawn move is the concrete answer.

Taking a pawn early is always wrong.

A centre pawn that really should be taken.
A developing move elsewhere is the point.

title: Opening lines and the structures they lead to

D0.outcome: Explains that openings lead to pawn structures and that structures dictate plans.

D1.outcome: Names the pawn structure reached by a given opening line and the typical plan of each side.

D2.outcome: Given a structure in an unlabeled position, recognises it and the plan even when reached by a different move order.

D3.outcome: Chooses between two move orders by the structure he wants and predicts the structure each leads to.

conditions: Rooks' files follow the pawn structure: the rooks' work is decided by the skeleton.

A transposition to a different structure.

title: Tempo: which moves helped

D0.outcome: Explains a tempo as a move that helped development, and that moving a piece twice, retreating, or making a forced reply costs one.

D1.outcome: In a short opening line, marks which moves helped and which cost a tempo.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled opening positions, picks the line that gains a tempo (a capture that forces a recapture, a developing move that attacks a piece already moved) over the one that loses it.

D3.outcome: Predicts when the count misleads (wasted moves, exceptions such as a6 in the Ruy Lopez) and explains why.

misconceptions: Any piece moved twice is bad.
More moves made means ahead in time.
conditions: Open or semi-open openings with contact between the sides.
Both sides play sensibly; the pawn move is not forced by a threat.
contrasts: Counting tempi mechanically: a piece moved twice to win material or freedom is justified.
A6 in the Ruy Lopez and h3 are justified non-developing moves.
Closed games develop more slowly and allow more pawn moves.

soft_prereq_notes.OPN.TRAPS.D1: tempo and trap decisions share the same positions

title: Opening traps and sure material

D0.outcome: Explains that a natural-looking capture or recapture in the opening can lose material, and states the beginner rule to take sure material.

D1.outcome: Told that a position is a trap, finds the poisoned capture and its refutation.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled opening positions, decides to capture or decline: takes sure material and declines the trap.

D3.outcome: Notices when the 'sure material' is itself the trap (a Legal-type recapture) and predicts the refutation.

misconceptions: Always take free material.
A trap needs a deep combination.
conditions: Beginner level; a concrete material gain is worth more than a speculative positional advantage.
contrasts: An offered pawn that loses material to a Legal-type trap.
Applying 'take sure material' when the sure material is itself the trap.
A developing move elsewhere.

title: Piece activity

D0.outcome: Explains piece activity as the number of useful squares a piece reaches and the lines it controls, not how far forward it stands.

D1.outcome: Picks the more active of two placements of the same piece and points out the squares or lines that make it so.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled quiet positions, picks the move that most improves the worst-placed piece ahead of pawn pushes, in at least 7 of 10.

D3.outcome: Predicts how a one-feature change (a pawn that opens a line, a trade that frees a rook) shifts the activity balance, and explains why an advanced piece can be less active than a retreated one.

D4.outcome: In own games, names the worst-placed piece before quiet moves, and the choices are shown in the review log.

misconceptions: A piece further forward is more active.
Activity means making threats on every move.
sources: sources/sheets/edlasker_chess-strategy.md §4 K5 (mobility is the value of a piece); §7 row K5
sources/sheets/emlasker_common-sense.md §4.7 (pawns that work vs pawns that merely need protection)
conditions: Mobility is the main criterion of a piece's worth in ordinary open or semi-open positions.
Central squares touch more of the board, so a piece there exerts more; the edge limits it.
A pawn move needs a purpose; a pawn that only needs protection is not working.
contrasts: A rook that wins the exchange but has no open file to enter gains no activity.
A knight on the rim after two moves has fewer squares than one on a central square.
A position decided by a forced tactic, where activity is moot.

soft_prereq_notes.OPN.PRINCIPLES.D1: development is the first form of activity

title: The bishop pair

D0.outcome: Explains why two bishops cover both colours of squares and when that matters (open lines, enemy knights without stations).

D1.outcome: In a given open position, chooses whether to keep the pair or trade a bishop for a knight and gives the structural reason.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled mixed positions, decides to keep or give up the pair, and does not apply 'never trade bishop for knight' blindly.

D3.outcome: Predicts how locking the centre or an unassailable knight post lowers the value of the pair, and decides a trade with the exchange rules.

misconceptions: Two bishops always beat two knights.
Trading a bishop for a knight early is always a mistake.
conditions: Open or semi-open lines and enemy knights without stations.
The long-range bishop is not traded for a knight early without compensation: the knight's power is limited to a circle.
contrasts: A closed position or an unassailable centrally posted knight lowers the pair's value.
'always a mistake' to trade a bishop for a pinned knight; this is routine in many structures.
A trade that is forced anyway.

soft_prereq_notes.FND.PIECE.KNIGHT.D1: the bishop-pair question is a comparison with the knight

title: Blockading a passed pawn

D0.outcome: Explains blockading as placing a supported piece on the square in front of a passed pawn so it cannot advance and its own pieces stay cramped.

D1.outcome: Chooses the blockading square and piece (a knight is the best default) for a given passed pawn.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, decides among blockading, watching from a distance or attacking the pawn, and supports the blockader.

D3.outcome: Predicts how the blockader's quality and elasticity change the plan, and when to exchange a strong blockader for a weaker one; knows a far-advanced passer may be better watched.

misconceptions: The blockade is obligatory for every passed pawn.
Blockade with whichever piece is nearest.
sources: docs/curriculum-map-v1.1.md §3 (POS.BLOCKADE: a default, not a duty)
conditions: The blockading piece is well supported; the pawn is dangerous or central.
Minor pieces make the best blockaders; the queen leaves at the first attack; the king is poor in the middlegame and useful in the endgame.
contrasts: A queen or king blockader that is exposed to attack.
'the blockade is obligatory' overreaches; a far-advanced passer may be better watched and a blockader can be overloaded.
A passed pawn that is already harmless.

soft_prereq_notes.POS.WEAKSQ.D2: the blockading square is a weak square for the pawn's owner

title: Pawn breaks and levers

D0.outcome: Explains a pawn break as an advance that offers an exchange to open lines or change the structure, judged by who profits from the opened line.

D1.outcome: Finds the break available to a side in a given structure and names the line it opens.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, chooses the break or the preparatory move, and says who benefits from the opened file or diagonal.

D3.outcome: Checks timing: whether the pieces are ready; predicts how a missing developing move or an extra defender makes the break premature.

misconceptions: Any break that opens a file is good for the side that has the rook on it.
A freeing break is good in every position.
conditions: The break is supported by development and not met by a pin tactic.
A pawn-protected obstruction is undermined with a lever, not battered.
contrasts: A lever that frees the opponent's pieces instead of fixing a target.
A break in an undeveloped position only exposes weaknesses.
A wing that offers no weaknesses (an attack there is hopeless).

title: Controlling the centre

D0.outcome: Explains that central control means influence over the central squares by pawns or pieces, and that pawns on e4 and d4 are one way and not the only way.

D1.outcome: Told to fight for the centre, picks the move that adds most to control of d4/e4/d5/e5 and names the pieces involved.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, decides whether to capture, support or ignore a central pawn offer by checking whether lines open for his pieces.

D3.outcome: Predicts how an exchange that gives up a central pawn can increase influence (opening the d-file and a diagonal), and when it cannot.

misconceptions: Pawns on e4 and d4 are the same as control of the centre.
Always take the offered centre pawn.

You are not behind in development and can recapture; what counts is opening lines toward the centre for your pieces.

title: The free mobile centre pawn

D0.outcome: Explains that an enemy mobile centre pawn is either removed by a prepared break or restrained until it is weak.

D1.outcome: Chooses between the quick kill (prepared break) and restraint (piece set-up) for a given free centre pawn.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, picks the break or set-up and rejects a premature break.

The centre must always be held by pawns.

contrasts: A premature break against the mobile pawn.
Holding the centre with pieces when a counterbalancing disadvantage appears.
No mobile centre pawn.

title: Connecting the rooks

D0.outcome: Explains that connecting the rooks (all minor pieces out and the queen off the back rank so the rooks see each other) completes development, and why that helps (mutual protection, doubling).

D1.outcome: In a position that looks winning, chooses among taking material, making a quiet threat, and exchanging, with the reason.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, notices when winning a pawn removes the key defender, and when simplifying is correct.

title: Dynamic play

title: Which trades help

title: True and illusory freeing moves

D0.outcome: Explains that a freeing move (usually a pawn break) is real only if the position can bear the opening of lines.

title: Good and bad pieces

D0.outcome: Explains that a bad piece is one with few useful squares or a poor role, and that a piece can be bad now and good later.

D1.outcome: Picks the worst piece of each side in a quiet position and says why (hemmed in by its own pawns, shut out, passive).

title: Imbalances checklist

title: Pawn majorities

Equal pawn counts on the wing.

A tactical position that needs no regrouping.

title: Obstructions

D0.outcome: Explains an obstruction as a low-value piece or pawn that blocks lines, easier to remove when it is the enemy's.

D1.outcome: In a given position, names the obstructions of both sides and the line each blocks.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, decides whether to remove an enemy obstruction, leave it, or use it, and removes his own blocked pawn by placing a piece under its protection.

D3.outcome: Predicts when an obstruction helps the attacker (a pawn sacrifice delaying castling; a queen as blockader).

misconceptions: Obstruction and blockade are two names for the same thing.
conditions: Enemy obstructions are easier to remove than your own blocked pawn.
contrasts: Obstruction helps the attacker (Morphy's pawn sacrifice that delays the enemy king from castling).
Using one vocabulary for obstruction and blockade.
An obstruction on a line that leads nowhere.

title: Open files

D0.outcome: Explains that an open file matters only if a rook can use it to reach an entry square on the seventh or eighth rank or attack a target.

D1.outcome: Told to use the open file, names the target pawn and the entry square and places the rook accordingly.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled middlegame positions, decides whether a file helps by naming its entry square and checking the square is not covered; decides whether opening a file helps him or the opponent.

D3.outcome: Chooses among the three ways past an obstructing pawn (batter, lever, sacrifice) by checking whether the pawn is protected, and counts attackers against defenders on it; uses a closed file as a jumping-off place when direct entry is shut.

D4.outcome: In own games, rook placements are recorded with the target and entry square named in the review log.

misconceptions: Occupying an open file is a goal in itself.
Any open file is good for whoever has a rook available.
sources: sources/sheets/edlasker_chess-strategy.md §4 K20 (open files, the seventh rank, being first), K12
conditions: Rooks present and an objective exists (a pawn to attack or an entry square).
The file is genuinely open and the entry squares are not controlled.
A pawn-protected obstruction is undermined with a lever; an unprotected one is besieged with more attackers than defenders; sacrifice only after the quiet methods and only for the entry.
contrasts: An open file whose entry squares are covered by a bishop, so winning the exchange gains nothing.
Opening a file that the opponent's rook can reach first.
A closed file that will not open.

title: Pieces out of play

D0.outcome: Explains that a piece can be out of play (shut in or far from the action) without being capturable.

D1.outcome: Finds the piece cut off from the action in a given position and says what cuts it off.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, classifies a piece as out of play, able to get out, or really trapped, and plans either to keep an enemy piece cut off or to free his own.

D3.outcome: Counts the cost of freeing a shut-in piece (a lever, an exchange) against the benefit of playing on the other wing while the enemy piece is idle.

misconceptions: A shut-in piece is a lost piece.
sources: docs/curriculum-map-v1.1.md §3 (POS.OUTOFPLAY as the contrast with TAC.TRAPPED)
conditions: The cut-off piece cannot be freed except at a cost.
contrasts: The piece can be freed by a sacrifice or an exchange.
Treating a temporarily blocked piece as lost without checking the defender's counter-sacrifices.
A well-placed piece elsewhere.

soft_prereq_notes.POS.EXCHANGE.D1: trading off the guard of the exit frees the piece

title: Outposts

D0.outcome: Explains an outpost as a piece on an advanced square that no enemy pawn can attack, usually supported by a pawn, with an open file or key squares behind it.

D1.outcome: Places a knight on a named outpost square and names the pawn that supports it and the squares it eyes.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, says whether a square is a real outpost for a named piece by checking the supporting pawn and that no enemy pawn can expel the piece.

D3.outcome: Predicts the effect of one-feature changes (the supporting pawn on e3 instead of e4; a lever that can dislodge the knight) and decides whether to trade the outpost piece.

misconceptions: A knight on the fifth rank is automatically an outpost.
An outpost is strong whatever the pawn structure behind it.
conditions: A protecting pawn is present, there is an open file or squares behind, and the opponent cannot kick the piece with a pawn without damage.
Its strength comes from its hinterland: remove the supporting pawn or the open file and it loses its point.
contrasts: Knight on d5 with the supporting pawn on e3 instead of e4, so the square is no longer a weakness for the enemy.
The enemy can expel the knight with a pawn lever.
The outpost has no useful targets from its square.

title: Over-protection

D0.outcome: Explains over-protecting a strategically important point as giving it more defence than the attack seems to need, so that the defenders become active by contact with it.

D1.outcome: In a given position, names the point that deserves over-protection and the pieces that will do it.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, decides whether a point should be over-protected or whether that would make the defenders passive.

D3.outcome: Predicts how the absence of pressure on the point turns over-protection into passive defence.

misconceptions: Over-protect everything.
Over-protection is the same as passive defence.
conditions: The point is strong and will come under pressure; the pieces involved do not become passive.
Practical, not proven; the examples are won games by a strong player (survivor bias).
contrasts: Over-protecting an ordinary weak point makes the defenders passive.
Over-protecting the base of a chain that needs no extra defence.
The point is under no pressure.

title: Passed pawns

D0.outcome: Explains that a passed pawn has no enemy pawn in front on its own or the adjacent files, and that it is strong only if it can be supported and is not blockaded.

D1.outcome: Identifies passed pawns for both sides, and counts the moves a passed pawn needs against the distance of the enemy king.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, decides whether to push, support or hold back a passed pawn, and notices which enemy piece it ties down.

D3.outcome: Predicts the effect of one-feature changes (a protected pawn, the quality of the blockader, a rook behind it) and says when pushing a passed pawn is premature.

misconceptions: A passed pawn must advance.
A passed pawn is always strong.
conditions: The pawn's whole path consists of squares the opponent cannot cheaply contest, so he must commit a man to watch it.
A passed pawn gains strength as pieces come off, but blockade, rook-pawns and activity matter.
contrasts: An isolated passed pawn can be a weakness rather than a strength.
Pushing the passer mechanically without asking what it ties down or whether the king can support it.
A passed pawn in a position decided by a king attack.

soft_prereq_notes.END.SQUARE.D1: counting whether the king catches the pawn

title: What does this pawn move leave behind?

D0.outcome: Explains that pawns cannot go back, so every pawn move changes which squares and pawns are guarded for the rest of the game.

D1.outcome: For a given pawn move, marks the squares it no longer guards and the pawns it leaves unprotected.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, judges whether a pawn move is safe given which enemy pieces can use the weakened squares, including harmless moves.

D3.outcome: Predicts consequences in front of a castled king, and how the same missing pawn matters differently in the middlegame and in the ending.

misconceptions: Pawn moves near the king are safer than piece moves.
Make a luft early as a precaution.
conditions: The opponent has pieces that can reach the weakened squares (a bishop of the right colour, a knight, a queen).
contrasts: The pawn move is fine when it forces off the opponent's attackers, or is needed (h3 against a pin, a forced luft).

The relevant enemy attackers are absent.

title: Pawn weaknesses

D0.outcome: Names isolated, doubled, backward and passed pawns in a position and says why each can be a weakness or a strength.

D1.outcome: Marks each pawn's type and the squares and pieces that make it a target.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, rates a pawn as a real weakness, harmless, or compensated, and chooses the plan; applies the stop-square condition for a backward pawn.

D3.outcome: Predicts how one feature (a neighbouring pawn, an open file, the bishop pair, the phase of the game) flips the verdict, and fixes then out-counts a backward pawn.

misconceptions: A weakness is a weakness in every phase.
Doubled pawns are always weak.
Every pawn behind its neighbours is backward and a target.
conditions: A backward pawn is a target when it cannot advance (the stop square is controlled), lies on a semi-open file, and the attacker's pieces have access.
Whether doubled or isolated pawns weaken depends on phase and piece activity; the bishop pair or an open file can compensate.
contrasts: A backward pawn that can advance safely, or whose stop square the opponent cannot reach, is not a target.
Backward pawns and holes 'invariably lead to disaster' (absolute wording; Sicilian and Hedgehog structures live with them).
The same weakness on a file the attacker cannot reach.

soft_prereq_notes.POS.PASSED.D1: the passed pawn is the opposite of a weakness

title: Pins as strategy: asking the question

D0.outcome: Explains that a pin can shape a whole game and that a pin is sometimes tolerated.

D1.outcome: Given a bishop pin on a knight, lists the four policies (put the question, ignore, bring up reserves, hold the choice) and says which suits the structure.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled opening positions, decides whether to ask the bishop (with a flank pawn push) by checking whether the centre can open.

D3.outcome: Predicts how a changed centre structure turns a good question into a weakening move.

misconceptions: The question always wins a tempo.
conditions: The question is good when the driven bishop lands on a desert that cannot be brought to life because the centre cannot be opened.
It is bad when the centre can open or the pawn advance leaves the king exposed to a break.
contrasts: The centre can open, so the bishop revives.
The question is disorganising for the side that asks it, so it needs compensation.
No pin on the board.

title: The key difference between the two sides

D0.outcome: Explains the difference method: list how the two sides differ (a pawn, a piece's diagonal, king position) because each difference suggests a possibility.

D1.outcome: In a near-symmetrical position, lists the three largest differences between the sides.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, identifies the difference that decides the plan, including one that favours the other side.

D3.outcome: Predicts how moving one feature (the king from g1 to b1, a pawn from a7 to b6) changes the verdict.

misconceptions: A difference automatically favours the side that has it.
conditions: The two sides are structurally similar; the method is weaker when everything differs.
The decisive character of a position is found among the objective differences, not a vague feel.
contrasts: A bishop that looks active on an open diagonal is the less useful placement.
Ahead on force, space and time, but the king on g1 instead of b1 makes a rook sacrifice win.
A difference that changes nothing about either side's plan.

soft_prereq_notes.POS.GOODBAD.D1: piece quality is one of the differences

title: Making a plan you can carry out

D0.outcome: Explains a plan as a direction supported by a feature of the position that the available pieces can carry out, revised when the opponent changes the position.

D1.outcome: For each side in a quiet position, names one plan that follows from a feature of the position (weak pawn, open file, space).

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, picks a move that belongs to a feasible plan and rejects a plan the available pieces cannot carry out.

D3.outcome: Explains why a plan fails when its feasibility condition breaks, and does not change plans without a reason.

misconceptions: Having a plan means pushing a pawn.
An unsound plan is better than none (not adopted).
sources: sources/sheets/edlasker_chess-strategy.md §4 K33; §7 row 'Plan vs none' (not adopted)
conditions: A plan is large-scale, promises success, is feasible with the means at hand, and advances only when concerted piece action can follow.
A plan is a general direction plus a guess at the opponent's main counter-moves, revised from time to time.
contrasts: 'an unsound plan carried through is better than no plan' (dated coaching advice).
Changing plans repeatedly without reason (irresolution).
A forced tactical position where no plan is needed.

title: Active, passive or neutral: mode follows the evaluation

D0.outcome: Explains that the right kind of game follows the valuation: better, play actively; worse, defend and restore freedom; equal, manoeuvre.

D1.outcome: Labels a position better, worse or equal and chooses the mode with a reason.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, picks the move that fits the mode, and does not attack from a clearly worse position or sit still when clearly better.

D3.outcome: Handles exceptions: counter-attack from a worse position; rejects the source's advice to give up when hopelessly worse.

misconceptions: Inferior means must be passive.
Resign when hopelessly worse (dated advice).
conditions: An honest valuation exists first (the hard part).
contrasts: Playing actively from an inferior position is the most dangerous choice, yet counter-attack remains the normal way out.
Playing passively from a superior position is the most wasteful.
A dead-equal position with no clear plan on either side.

soft_prereq_notes.ATK.PACE.D1: mode and pace of an attack are linked

title: Allocating pieces to the plan

D0.outcome: Explains deciding where the main blow falls, which pieces can be spared for it, and the minimum number needed for defence.

D1.outcome: In a position with a target, names the pieces for the attack, the pieces to keep for defence, and the order of arrival.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, avoids sending every piece to the attack and keeps defenders that also serve the plan.

D3.outcome: Predicts the effect of a miscount of defenders, and mixes short-range and long-range pieces in the order of arrival.

misconceptions: All pieces should rush to the attack.
conditions: There is a definite target (the king, a weak pawn).
Defenders that also serve the centre are preferred (knight on f3 and bishop on g2).
contrasts: Reserving only the 'necessary' defenders when the count of defenders is wrong.
Short-range pieces brought in first are driven off before the plan matures.
No definite target yet, so no allocation question.

soft_prereq_notes.ATK.CASTLED.D1: piece allocation is clearest in a king attack

title: Racing plans

D0.outcome: Explains comparing the number of moves each side's plan needs, and that forcing replies can break the count.

D1.outcome: For two flank plans, counts the moves each needs and says who arrives first.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, decides between counter-attack and defence, and checks for forcing moves that break the count.

D3.outcome: Predicts how a single check or tempo move changes the count.

misconceptions: The shorter plan wins automatically.
conditions: The plans are clear, mostly forcing, with few intermediate options.
contrasts: The count ignores intermediate checks and the opponent's replies, so the claimed 'seven moves versus five' fails.
A clean count spoiled by a forcing check.
A position where a tactic dominates.

title: Prophylaxis

D0.outcome: Explains prophylaxis as asking what the opponent wants to play and preventing his useful or freeing moves, and says it is not passivity.

D1.outcome: In a given position, names the opponent's real freeing move and the move that prevents it.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, chooses between executing his own plan and first removing the opponent's counterplay, and leaves it alone when the opponent has no real threat.

D3.outcome: Separates the two forms (preventing the freeing move; bringing pieces into contact with strategic points) and predicts when the prophylactic move costs a decisive tempo.

misconceptions: Prophylaxis is passivity.
A quiet move needs a threat to be useful.
sources: sources/sheets/nimzowitsch_my-system.md §4 ideas 32-33; §9 (scope broader than his two forms)
conditions: The opponent's freeing move is real.
A preparatory move pays when the opponent's threat is genuine and the position lets him execute it.
contrasts: A prophylactic move against a threat that cannot be executed wastes a tempo.
With no target yet, ignoring the opponent's preparations is better (defence by waiting).
The opponent has no freeing move in the position.

title: Re-evaluating after changes

D0.outcome: Explains that an evaluation must be updated after exchanges, pawn breaks and tactics, and that the old plan may no longer fit.

D1.outcome: After a stated change in a position, restates which imbalance changed and what plan now fits.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled sequences, spots the move that changes the evaluation and re-picks the plan instead of continuing the old one.

D3.outcome: Notices when a habit-driven plan is continuing after the position changed, and does a fresh valuation as a spectator would.

misconceptions: A plan chosen at move 12 stays valid at move 30.
conditions: A concrete change (exchange, break, tactic) has altered the imbalances.
contrasts: Sticking to the old plan after a pawn break changed the structure (thinking inertia).
Changing plans constantly without a changed position.
A position unchanged since the last evaluation.

title: Restraint

D0.outcome: Explains restraint as stopping an enemy pawn break before it happens: first restrain, next blockade, lastly destroy.

D1.outcome: Chooses the set-up that restrains a given mobile pawn or majority and names the break it prevents.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, decides whether the break is real enough to justify a restraining set-up such as a rook on a still-closed file.

D3.outcome: Predicts when restraint stops working against a break whose time has come.

misconceptions: A rook belongs on an open file at once, never on a closed one.
conditions: The enemy pawn break is real, and the structure allows the set-up.
contrasts: Restraint cannot hold forever against a freeing move whose time has come.
A rook on a closed file with no break to deter.
No real break to restrain.

title: The seventh rank

D0.outcome: Explains why a rook on the seventh attacks pawns from behind and confines the king, and that this is strongest when the rank is protected and the king is cut off.

D1.outcome: Told to invade the seventh, finds the entry square and the targets on the rank (pawns, fork squares).

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, decides whether to invade now, double the rooks first, or not at all; notices a fork on the seventh.

D3.outcome: Tells apart the special cases (king cut off with an advanced passer, two rooks giving perpetual check, rook and knight apparatus) and checks that the rank is really absolute before counting on a win.

misconceptions: A rook on the seventh rank is always winning.
Any route to the seventh counts as using the file.
conditions: The enemy is cramped on the rank, has few defenders there, and the way in is safe.
The rank is 'absolute' only if the enemy king is confined behind it (with an advanced passer, wins almost always).
contrasts: A rook on the seventh while the king can step out is only a draw.
A catastrophic invasion arises from the opponent's serious mistakes; in normal play the seventh is mostly an endgame asset.
A rook on the seventh rank with nothing there to attack.

title: Space and restriction

D0.outcome: Explains a space advantage as having more safe squares and posts for pieces behind advanced pawns, one that persists without needing immediate threats.

D1.outcome: In a given position, says who has more space and which enemy pieces lack safe squares.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, picks quiet restriction (deny the freeing break) over a showy threat, and watches for the liberating sacrifice or exchange.

D3.outcome: Predicts when space becomes a liability (overextended pawns become targets) and which break frees the cramped side.

misconceptions: Space must be backed by piece activity everywhere.
Restriction is passivity.
sources: sources/sheets/znosko-borovsky_middle-game.md §5 item 9 (space can keep growing is overstated)
conditions: The opponent's pieces really have no safe squares and no pawn break.
Unlike a time lead, a space lead does not decay; but watch for a liberating sacrifice by the strangled side.
contrasts: The same space, but a freeing pawn lever exists.
'a space advantage can keep growing without limit' is overstated; breaks and counter-sacrifices undermine it.
An opened position where space does not matter.

title: Real and fictitious threats
origin: map-v1.1 (idea named in MAP11 §3 without an id; the id SAF.FICTITIOUS is ours)

D0.outcome: Explains the difference between a capture that gains something after best play and one that only looks possible, and gives one reason a capture can be fictitious (pin, discovered line, recapture).

D1.outcome: In positions where a piece is attacked, says whether the attack is real and states the reason when it is not.

D2.outcome: In a mixed set that includes harmless moves, says for each of the opponent's last moves whether it threatens anything, without being told to look for a bluff.

D3.outcome: Finds the quiet move that makes the opponent's real threat fictitious (removing the checking line or the pinned target) and says what it costs in tempo; rejects it when the threat could not be carried out anyway.

misconceptions: Any attacked piece is threatened.
A threat that cannot be executed now can be ignored for good (the position changes and the same capture may work three moves later).
A preparatory move to disarm a threat is always a wasted tempo.
conditions: A threat is real if carrying it out gains something against best defence; it is fictitious if the capture loses to a pin, discovered line or recapture.
A fictitious threat still ties the opponent and becomes real the moment it is forgotten.
A move that removes the opponent's counterplay first pays only when his threat is genuine and he can execute it.
contrasts: A piece left en prise is safe for a few moves; later the same capture works because the position changed.
Spending a tempo to disarm a threat that did not exist (prophylaxis as passivity).
A position with nothing attacked; the correct answer is that there is no threat.
