title: Loose pieces

D0.outcome: Says that in this course a loose piece is one that an enemy piece attacks and none of its own side defends, and why it is in danger.

D1.outcome: When told 'find the loose pieces', taps every attacked piece that has no defender (kings do not count).

D2.outcome: With no announcement, says how many of its pieces are loose, including none.

D3.outcome: Before each move checks both sides' pieces, and notices pieces that become loose only after a move or an exchange.

misconceptions: A piece is safe because nothing attacks it right now.
A defended piece can never be lost.
A piece nobody attacks is in danger just because nothing defends it.
conditions: A piece is loose when an enemy piece attacks it and none of its own side's pieces defends it.
Check the pieces one by one; kings are not counted.
contrasts: A piece that is attacked but defended is not loose, although the exchange may still go against it (see SAF.COUNT).
A piece that nobody attacks is not loose even if nothing defends it.

title: What does their last move threaten?

D0.outcome: Says that before moving you ask what the opponent's last move threatens: a capture, a check, a mate.

D1.outcome: When told 'what does the opponent threaten?', names the capture or the mate that is threatened.

D2.outcome: In mixed positions finds the opponent's threat when there is one and says 'none' when there is none.

D3.outcome: Finds double threats, and checks that a reply stops the threat without creating a new weakness.

misconceptions: Only captures count as threats; checks and mates do not.
If the last move attacks nothing, there is no threat.
conditions: After the opponent's move ask: what could they capture, check or mate next move if I did nothing?
Sometimes the answer is 'nothing': say so.
contrasts: A quiet-looking developing move can threaten mate in one.
A move that attacks nothing of yours is not a threat; do not invent a reply to it.

title: Self-direction 1: observe

D0.outcome: Explains that observing means noting what happened before judging it.

D1.outcome: After the first game, marks one moment he was unsure and states what he expected the opponent to do.

D2.outcome: After three consecutive games, marks an unsure moment and his expectation of the opponent unprompted, each specific to that game.

D3.outcome: After a game, compares his expectation with what the opponent actually did and says so in one sentence.

misconceptions: Reflection means saying whether I played well.
sources: docs/first-hours.md session 3 (reflection before engine commentary), 'What would show this does or doesn't work'
conditions: The reflection comes before any engine commentary.
contrasts: An empty or generic answer ('it was fine'): the prompt is too abstract and needs a concrete question.
Reflecting after engine output, which anchors the answer.
A game of three moves ending in a disconnect.
contrast_sources: FH, what would show this does not work
note: A played game is a session milestone, not a node; D1 depends on FND.CAPTURE.D1 as the weakest rules prerequisite.

title: Self-direction 2: explain

D0.outcome: Explains why explaining a move to oneself helps and gives an example.

D1.outcome: States in one sentence why he chose a move at five stops in a game.

D2.outcome: Gives explanations that name a feature of the position (not 'it looked good') in at least 7 of 10 positions.

D3.outcome: Explains a move together with an alternative he considered and why he rejected it.

misconceptions: Explaining a move means restating it.
conditions: The explanation is written before the result is known.
contrasts: An explanation that restates the move ('I moved the knight').
A post-hoc rationalisation after seeing the result.
A forced move with nothing to explain.

title: Self-direction 3: diagnose

D0.outcome: Explains the difference between a gap in knowledge and a gap in performance, using the cue ladder as evidence.

D1.outcome: From his own ledger, names one recurring gap and the evidence for it.

D2.outcome: Shows, for at least one concept, the gap between explaining it and finding it unlabeled, and says which step failed.

D3.outcome: Distinguishes a process gap from a knowledge gap and proposes a test for each.

misconceptions: If I can explain it I can find it.
sources: docs/reconciliation-pasted-curriculum.md §2 (knowledge versus performance, adopted into SELF.3)
conditions: Evidence comes from the learner's own cue-level data and games.
contrasts: Diagnosing from one game.
Blaming luck for a repeating error.
A gap in a concept not yet taught.

title: Self-direction 4: plan with support

D0.outcome: Explains the plan, do, review cycle and why a review date is part of the plan.

D1.outcome: With a template, writes a four-week plan with one target concept, a weekly load and a review date.

D2.outcome: At the review date, revises the plan from evidence, changing one thing for a stated reason.

D3.outcome: Completes two plan, do, review cycles with the support fading.

misconceptions: A plan with many goals is a better plan.
conditions: The plan names one target and a review date.
contrasts: Ten goals and no load limit.
A plan unchanged despite contrary evidence.
A plan for a skill that is already mastered.

title: Self-direction 5: experiment

D0.outcome: Explains a one-variable experiment on his own training.

D1.outcome: Designs one (for example two weeks interleaved against two weeks blocked) and states what result would change his mind.

D2.outcome: Runs his designed experiment, records the data, and reports the result with the sample size.

D3.outcome: Decides to keep or drop the change from the data, not from preference.

misconceptions: Two sessions show whether a method works.
conditions: One variable changes at a time and the sample is stated.
contrasts: Changing three things at once.
Concluding from two sessions.
A change that cannot be measured.

title: Self-direction 6: lead

D0.outcome: Explains independent practice with declining assistance and the idea of a silent session.

D1.outcome: Writes and runs his own training manual for a month with no system prompts.

D2.outcome: Completes silent sessions in which unprompted behaviours stay stable.

D3.outcome: Chooses which skills to hand back to coached mode on the evidence.

misconceptions: Independence comes with rating.
sources: docs/council-synthesis.md Round 11, CD-11 (the four roles; role fading by evidence, not rating; Guardian study, finding not independently checked)
conditions: Roles fade by evidence of unprompted competence, not by rating.
contrasts: Independence declared because of a rating.
Solitary self-directed work is not automatically good (group practice mattered in one study).
A skill still at the cued stage.

title: Self-direction 7: investigate

D0.outcome: Explains the shape of an original chess question and how it can be tested.

D1.outcome: Poses a question (a dated claim from a source) and designs a test using an engine or tablebase.

D2.outcome: Completes a test of his question and writes a conclusion that another person reviews.

D3.outcome: Publishes a reusable exercise family with verified claims.

misconceptions: Research means looking for a novelty.
sources: docs/reconciliation-pasted-curriculum.md §2 (Dvoretsky Endgame Analysis as a model)
conditions: Claims are verified and the limits recorded.
contrasts: A conclusion without a limit or a failing look-alike.
A test that cannot fail.
A question already answered by a tablebase lookup.

title: Back-rank mates

D0.outcome: Explains why a king behind its own unmoved pawns can be mated on its first rank by a single rook or queen check.

D1.outcome: When told 'find the back-rank mate', finds it, including with a preceding capture or exchange that removes a guard.

D2.outcome: In mixed sets, finds the back-rank mate for either side, and spots when his own back rank is the weakness, with no theme named.

D3.outcome: Counts the defenders of the back rank, finds the exchange or deflection that removes the last one, and decides whether to make air for the king now or later.

misconceptions: Making air for the king (a luft) early is always wise.
A back-rank mate needs a rook; a queen or two minor pieces can finish too.
sources: sources/sheets/nimzowitsch_my-system.md §4 ideas 7, 21 (queen checks on the eighth; exchanges that win by back-rank mate)
sources/sheets/edlasker_chess-strategy.md §4 K6 (d), K17 (b) (a luft is correct once a mate threat shows, not before)
conditions: The king is boxed by its own pawns with no flight square and no piece guards the first rank.
The checking piece cannot be captured, and the check cannot be blocked.
A series of exchanges can remove the last guard and end in the mate.
contrasts: The defender has a flight square, an interposition or a guarding rook, so the 'mate' is only a check.
Making a luft as a precaution long before a mate threat exists costs time and loosens the king's cover.
A castled king with a luft already open or a pawn moved is not subject to this mate.

soft_prereq_notes.FND.CASTLE.D1: castling is how the king gets boxed in

title: Clearance

D0.outcome: Explains clearance as moving a piece away, often with a threat, to open a square or line for another piece.

D1.outcome: When told to clear the line or square, finds the vacating move that uses a tempo-gaining threat.

D2.outcome: In mixed sets, finds clearances that win or mate and avoids those that merely retreat.

D3.outcome: Checks that the vacating move comes with a threat the opponent must answer, and predicts the effect of removing that threat.

misconceptions: Any move that opens a line is a clearance.
sources: sources/sheets/nimzowitsch_my-system.md §4 idea 29 (masking piece free to attack)
conditions: The vacating move carries its own threat so that the opponent has no time to cover the cleared line.
contrasts: The vacating move has no threat and the opponent closes the line.
The cleared square is covered by a defender that also attacks the vacated piece.
Moving a piece away when the line it blocks leads nowhere.

soft_prereq_notes.TAC.DISCOVER.D2: a clearance is a discovered attack made on purpose

note: No synthesis sheet covers this motif; conditions are ours.

title: Multi-motif combinations

D0.outcome: Explains a combination as a chain of forcing moves, each justified by the one after it, and says why the whole chain must be checked and not only its first move.

D1.outcome: Given that a combination exists, finds a two-motif sequence (for example a deflection followed by a mating pattern).

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, finds a three-move combination when one exists and says there is none when the apparent combination fails at the last step.

D3.outcome: Checks each branch of the combination including the declined lines and the quiet defensive reply, and predicts which one-feature change breaks it.

misconceptions: A combination that works against passive defence works against the best defence.
A complicated combination is better than a simple winning move.
sources: sources/sheets/capablanca_chess-fundamentals.md §4 CI-27, CI-29, CI-32 (the simple winning move may be preferable); CI-51 (G2: a combination judged unsound without its quiet follow-up)
conditions: Each step is forced or clearly best, and the final position is checked for the opponent's quiet replies.
The complicated course is highly risky until one has wide experience, and the simple winning move may be preferable.
contrasts: The combination works against one defence, but a quiet follow-up for the defender refutes it.
A simple winning move exists and the combination adds only risk.
A quiet position with no forcing resources for either side.

soft_prereq_notes.TAC.DEFLECT.D2: deflection drags away the defender that the chain depends on

title: Decoy

D0.outcome: Explains a decoy as luring a piece, often the king, to a square where it can be attacked or mated.

D1.outcome: When told 'find the decoy', finds the sacrifice that forces a piece to the target square.

D2.outcome: In mixed sets, finds the decoy that wins or mates, and rejects offers the opponent can refuse.

D3.outcome: Verifies that the capture is forced or best, and that the follow-up works against every non-capturing reply; predicts how one extra defender kills it.

misconceptions: A sacrificed piece must be taken.
sources: sources/sheets/capablanca_chess-fundamentals.md §4 CI-27, CI-29 (queen, knight, bishop sacrifices that open the king's cover)
sources/sheets/nimzowitsch_my-system.md §4 idea 19 (a remote passer as a decoy)
conditions: The capture is forced or clearly the best of the replies.
The lured piece lands on a square from which the follow-up wins at once.
contrasts: The sacrifice can be declined and the attacker has nothing else.
The lured king escapes along a flight square the follow-up does not cover.
A sacrifice that wins the same material without luring anything.

soft_prereq_notes.TAC.DOUBLE-CHECK.D1: decoy sacrifices often end in a double-check mate

title: Deflection

D0.outcome: Explains deflection as forcing a defending piece away from its post by capture, check or threat.

D1.outcome: When told 'deflect the defender', finds the move that drags the defender from the key square.

D2.outcome: In mixed sets, finds the deflection that wins material or mates, and does not play it when the defender can decline or the offered piece can be left alone.

D3.outcome: Verifies the declined line: what happens if the defender ignores the offer, and predicts how the position changes when the deflected piece has an alternative post.

misconceptions: The defender must accept the deflecting capture.
sources: sources/sheets/capablanca_chess-fundamentals.md §4 CI-27, CI-29 (sacrifices that open the king's cover; imitate only with the follow-up checked)
conditions: Accepting is forced, or declining loses something else.
The key square or duty becomes undefended the moment the defender leaves.
contrasts: The defender declines the offered piece and keeps guarding.
Another piece takes over the duty after the deflection.
Deflecting a piece that was not guarding anything important.
contrast_sources: CAP CI-29 (g): sacrifice imitated without checking the follow-up

soft_prereq_notes.TAC.FORK.D2: deflecting a defender often opens a fork

title: Desperado pieces

D0.outcome: Explains a desperado as a piece that is lost anyway and so captures as much as it can before it falls.

D1.outcome: When told there is a desperado, finds the sequence of captures by the doomed piece.

D2.outcome: In mixed exchange positions, spots a doomed piece and chooses between saving it and selling it dearly.

D3.outcome: Counts the whole sequence with the desperado's captures and the recaptures; predicts how a defended capture target changes the count.

misconceptions: A doomed piece should simply retreat if it can.
sources: sources/sheets/nimzowitsch_my-system.md §4 idea 21 (selling a doomed queen dearly); §7 row 21
conditions: The piece is lost in any case and has captures available.
contrasts: The piece is not really lost; a retreat saves it and the captures lose the exchange.
Each capture the desperado makes allows a recapture that wins more than it took.
A doomed piece with no capture available.

soft_prereq_notes.TAC.TRAPPED.D2: a trapped piece is the usual desperado

title: Discovered attacks and checks

D0.outcome: Describes a discovered attack (moving one piece uncovers a line of another) and says why the moving piece is free to make a second threat.

D1.outcome: When told 'find the discovered check or attack', finds the masking-piece move that uncovers it and says what the moved piece attacks.

D2.outcome: In mixed sets, finds the discovered attack that wins material or mates, and does not play it when the opponent's reply captures the uncovering piece or blocks the line.

D3.outcome: Chooses the best move for the masking piece (capture, strongest threat, or the move that sets up a see-saw) and checks that the uncovered line cannot be interposed.

misconceptions: The moving piece must have a harmless job; it can attack or capture anything.
A discovered check always wins material.
conditions: A discovered check is a pin in which the pinned piece has changed sides: the masking piece can capture anything, attack anything or relocate, and cannot be recaptured because the opponent is in check.
It works best against a king with few flight squares.
The see-saw: a piece that checks from one square and discovers a check from another wins material with every swing because the king has only one move.
contrasts: A discovered attack on a non-king target, which the opponent answers with a counter-threat or by moving the target with a gain of tempo.
The discovered line can be interposed by a piece that also attacks the masking piece.
The masking piece's departure uncovers a line to a square where nothing of the opponent stands.

soft_prereq_notes.TAC.PIN.D1: a discovered check is a pin in which the pinned piece has changed sides (Nimz #29)
soft_prereq_notes.TAC.FORK.D1: the masking piece usually makes a second threat, as in a fork

title: Double check

D0.outcome: Explains why a double check can only be answered by a king move.

D1.outcome: When told 'find the double check', finds the move that gives it and lists the king's only legal replies.

D2.outcome: In mixed sets, finds the double check that mates or wins material and says 'no double check' where none exists.

D3.outcome: Combines a double check with a discovered see-saw or a queen sacrifice, and verifies that every king flight loses.

misconceptions: Interposing or capturing can answer a double check.
A double check always mates.
sources: sources/sheets/nimzowitsch_my-system.md §4 idea 29 (double check leaves only flight; he calls it purely tactical)
conditions: Both checks arise from one move (a discovered check plus the moving piece's own check); only a king move is legal.
It decides the game when every flight square is covered or leads to a worse position.
contrasts: The king has a safe flight square, and the double check merely drives it to a better square.
A single check with a blockable line mistaken for a double check.
A double check available in a position where the king has an immediate mating threat of its own is not the point.

soft_prereq_notes.FND.PIECE.KING.D1: the king's flight squares decide whether a double check mates

title: Forks (double attacks)

D0.outcome: States that one move can attack two valuable things so that only one can be saved, and says what must be true for the fork to win material (the forking square is safe; no single reply meets both threats).

D1.outcome: When told 'find the fork', finds the knight, queen, pawn or king fork in a simple position.

D2.outcome: Finds an available fork in a mixed set where no theme is named, answers 'no fork' where there is none, and does not play a fork-looking move that fails.

D3.outcome: Checks whether a fork really wins material: recapture on the forking square, a check that saves both targets, a target that captures the forker; predicts which one-feature change turns a working fork into a failing one.

D4.outcome: In own games, takes available forks and avoids leaving a fork for the opponent; the opportunity log shows the rate of available forks taken over ten games.

D5.outcome: Builds a working / failing / irrelevant trio for the fork and explains the deciding feature to a peer; repairs a faulty fork exercise.

misconceptions: A fork always wins material (ignores a defended forking square or a trapped forking piece).
Only knights fork.
Two attacked pieces that protect each other are forked.
sources: docs/first-hours.md session 5 (cue ladder in miniature; I-FORK-001/002/003)
sources/sheets/znosko-borovsky_middle-game.md §4 C26 (a knight's attack cannot be returned except by a knight), §8 idea 11
conditions: The forking square is safe: it is not attacked by something cheaper, or the capture there costs the capturer more.
No single reply parries both threats: no capture of the forker, no interposition, no check that gains the tempo.
A knight cannot be captured by the piece it attacks unless that piece is a knight, so a knight fork on a queen, rook or king cannot be answered by taking the forker with the target.
contrasts: Same fork shape with the king one square over, so the forking square is covered and the knight is lost for a pawn.
Both forked pieces are defended and worth less than the forker, so the 'fork' wins only an exchange or nothing.
Two pieces are attacked but only one is worth capturing and the other protects it; the move has no extra effect.

soft_prereq_notes.SAF.THREAT.D1: what the last move attacks often points to the fork square

title: Interference

D0.outcome: Explains interference as placing a piece on the line between two enemy pieces so they no longer support each other.

D1.outcome: When told to interfere, finds the interposing move that cuts a defender from its target or a guard from its square.

D2.outcome: In mixed sets, finds interferences that win material or mate, and rejects those where the interposed piece is simply captured with gain.

D3.outcome: Checks what the interposed piece costs and whether the opponent can use the line again, and predicts how an extra protector refutes it.

misconceptions: The interposed piece is safe because it is protected.
conditions: The interposed piece is safe or its capture opens something worse for the opponent.
The cut line was essential to the defence.
contrasts: The interposed piece is taken with tempo and the line is restored.
The cut line was not essential because another defender covers the square.
Placing a piece between two enemy pieces that never supported each other.

title: Mating patterns

D0.outcome: Explains what must be true for a check to be mate: the king's squares are covered or blocked, the checker cannot be taken, the check cannot be blocked.

D1.outcome: When told the family (back-rank, smothered, corner knight with a queen, two bishops on adjacent diagonals, queen next to the king), finds the mate in one or two.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, finds mate in one or two when it exists and says 'no mate' where it does not.

D3.outcome: Given a pattern on the board, says which single piece or pawn, if removed, breaks it, and verifies a sacrifice leading to the pattern against the declined lines.

misconceptions: A queen sacrifice near the king always works.
A pattern learned from a diagram works in any position that looks similar.
sources: sources/sheets/capablanca_chess-fundamentals.md §4 CI-27 (combination types around a castled king), CI-49 (a Legal-type trap, outside knowledge); §7 row 28
conditions: Every flight square is covered or blocked, the checker is immune to capture, and the line cannot be intercepted.
A queen, rook or minor-piece sacrifice works when it opens the king's cover and the co-ordinated pieces cover the weak point.
contrasts: The pattern is nearly there but one flight square is open, so the check is not mate.
The sacrifice is the same but a defender covers the key square.
A position with a mating pattern for the other side only.
contrast_sources: CAP CI-27 (g): no failing look-alike in the book, so we supply it

title: Searching for a forced mate

D0.outcome: Explains that a forced mate is found by listing, not by hoping: every check first, then every quiet move after which each reply of the defender allows mate, and that 'no forced mate here' is a valid answer.

D1.outcome: Told 'mate in two' with a check as the first move, lists the defender's replies (capture the checker, block, step away) and finds the mating answer to each.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions lists every check and every quiet move that might leave no defence, finds the mate in two when it exists, and answers 'no forced mate in two' by naming the refutation of each candidate.

D3.outcome: Finds mates in three, including a quiet first move, and tests each defender reply (a counter-check, the capture of the mating piece, a move that makes a flight square) before claiming the mate; recognises strong attacks where no mate exists.

D4.outcome: In own games, the opportunity log shows forced mates found when they were available, and no mate-looking attack played that the defender could simply refuse; the search is run for the opponent's threats as well as for the own attack.

misconceptions: If every check fails there is no mate (quiet first moves are skipped).
A move that threatens mate is as good as a mate.
A queen next to the king means mate is near.
Listing only the attacker's moves is enough (the defender's counter-check or capture of the mating piece is forgotten).
sources: docs/skill-graph.md section 6, gap 1 (the gap this node closes; mate in one or two was folded into TAC.MATE-PATTERNS D2)
sources/sheets/emlasker_common-sense.md §4.14 (a king commands up to nine squares: the flight-square count)
sources/sheets/capablanca_chess-fundamentals.md §4 CI-27 (combination types around a castled king)

conditions: A first move that gives check is a mate in two only if every legal reply (capturing the checker, blocking, or moving the king) can be answered by a mating move; list the replies from the rules instead of guessing them.

Search in a fixed order: all checks, then captures next to the king, then quiet moves that remove a flight square or a defender; answer 'no forced mate' only after the list is used up.
The defender's best replies are the forcing ones: a check, the capture of the attacking piece, or an interposition that makes a mate threat of its own; they must be listed before the mate is claimed.

The same attack with one more defender that covers the key square, so the quiet move no longer leaves the king without a defence.

title: Is there a tactic at all?

D0.outcome: Says that many positions in real games contain no tactic, and states what to do then (a safe developing move or a plan).

D1.outcome: In a themed set where each position may or may not contain the named tactic, answers yes or no and finds the move when yes.

D2.outcome: In mixed unlabeled sets where about four in ten positions have no tactic and some contain a familiar pattern that fails, answers 'none' correctly and finds the actual best move when a different tactic exists.

D3.outcome: Calculates a familiar pattern to its refutation, states the fault (a covered forking square, a luft), and finds the better move that the familiar answer hides.

D4.outcome: In own games, the opportunity log shows both the missed-tactic rate and the false-alarm rate, reported with the sample size, over ten games.

misconceptions: Every position contains a tactic if I look hard enough.
If I see a pattern I know, it must work.

conditions: Transfer, not fluency, is what counts: only unlabeled items with no-tactic and failing-pattern positions test it.
A familiar solution can block a better one, even for experts.
contrasts: The full mating pattern is on the board, but a defender covers a flight square.
Hunting for a tactic in a position where a quiet developing move is best.
A position where the side to move is in check, so the only question is how to answer.

soft_prereq_notes.LOOP.V2.D2: the forcing-move list is the quick test for whether anything exists

note: Map: runs through every tier. Modelled as one node at tier 3 that unlabeled sets from every tactic node point at.

title: Overloaded defenders

D0.outcome: Explains that a defender with two duties can be beaten by attacking one so the other is abandoned.

D1.outcome: When told 'find the overloaded piece', finds the piece and the capture or check that exploits it.

D2.outcome: In mixed sets, finds the overload that wins material, and does not play it when the two duties lie on one line or can be met by one move.

D3.outcome: Lists every duty of a defender before concluding it is overloaded, and predicts how an interposition or a third defender removes the effect.

misconceptions: A piece that defends two things is always overloaded.
sources: sources/sheets/edlasker_chess-strategy.md §4 K3 (ii) (a defender forced away by a bigger threat; a mate threat ties down a piece)
conditions: Both duties are needed at once and cannot be met by one move.
The attacker's exploiting move forces a decision (a capture or check) rather than merely hinting.
contrasts: Both duties lie on the same line, so one move of the defender serves both.
An interposition meets the second threat without moving the defender.
A piece with two jobs whose second job is not needed in this position.

soft_prereq_notes.SAF.COUNT.D2: the count shows where one defender has two jobs

title: Perpetual check

D0.outcome: Explains perpetual check as a sequence of checks the king cannot escape and that repeats the position.

D1.outcome: When told 'find the perpetual', finds the checking sequence and shows the repetition.

D2.outcome: In mixed sets, finds the perpetual for the worse side, and tests the king's escape squares before relying on it.

D3.outcome: Decides whether to take the perpetual or play on, verifying the king cannot escape the checks and that a better winning try does not exist; predicts how one extra defender or flight square breaks it.

misconceptions: A series of checks is a perpetual without testing where the king can go.
A perpetual is always the best result for the worse side, and the better side should always accept it.
sources: sources/sheets/emlasker_common-sense.md §4.16 (does the perpetual exist? the champion's own error); §8 idea 9
sources/sheets/nimzowitsch_my-system.md §4 idea 13 (two rooks on the seventh; rook and knight apparatus)
sources/sheets/capablanca_chess-fundamentals.md §5 item 21 (engines often show taking the repetition)
conditions: The king has no escape from the checks, the checking piece cannot be blocked or captured, and checks repeat.
Two rooks on the seventh rank keep checking if the guarding rook stays as the sentinel.
contrasts: The checking sequence ends when the king reaches a square the checker cannot follow, so no perpetual exists.
The perpetual exists but the stronger side can avoid it by interposing or by a tactic.
A position where the worse side has a better practical try than a draw.

soft_prereq_notes.POS.SEVENTH.D3: two rooks on the seventh give a perpetual check

title: Pins

D0.outcome: Describes a pin (a piece that cannot move, or should not, because a more valuable piece stands behind it on the same line) and the difference between a pin against the king and a pin against another piece.

D1.outcome: When told 'find the pin', finds the move that pins a piece and says what is pinned to what.

D2.outcome: In mixed sets with no theme named, finds the pin that wins material or a tempo, notices that an enemy defender is pinned so its protection is imaginary, and answers 'no pin' where there is none.

D3.outcome: Judges whether a pin is real: a piece that may legally slide along the line, recapture options, a king escape; wins the pinned piece by adding attackers or attacking it with a pawn; predicts how one extra defender changes the result.

D4.outcome: In own games, uses pins and deals with enemy pins (breaks the pin or tolerates it on purpose), shown by the opportunity log over ten games.

misconceptions: Any pin wins a piece.
A pinned piece cannot move at all (a half-pinned piece may slide along the pinning line; a piece pinned to a non-king may legally move).
A pinned defender still protects the square it guards.
conditions: The pin is genuine: the piece behind is the king or worth more, and there is no tactical escape.

A piece pinned to the king cannot capture, so its protection of a square is imaginary and a piece may stand where only that pinned piece guards it; for a pin against a lesser piece the protection is real only if giving up the rear piece pays.
Win a pinned piece by multiplying attackers; the best attacker is a pawn because the pinned piece cannot flee.
contrasts: A half-pin: the pinned piece slides along the pin line, so it is not wholly pinned.
A pin against a non-king piece where moving the pinned piece costs less than the loss assumed, or recapture is available.
Two pieces share a line but the front one is worth more than the rear one, which is a skewer rather than a pin.

soft_prereq_notes.SAF.LOOSE.D2: a loose piece is the natural target of a pin

title: The quiet move in a combination

D0.outcome: Explains why a move with no check, capture or direct threat can be the key to a combination.

D1.outcome: When told there is a quiet move, finds the move that creates an unstoppable threat or removes the defender's last resource.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, finds the quiet move when forcing moves fail, and does not play one when a forcing win exists.

D3.outcome: Verifies that the quiet move leaves the opponent no useful check or capture in reply, and predicts what a single spare tempo for the defender does to it.

misconceptions: A move that does not force anything cannot win.
A grand combination is better than a slow correct move.
sources: sources/sheets/capablanca_chess-fundamentals.md §4 CI-51 (G4: looking for a grand combination, rejecting a slow correct move)
sources/sheets/znosko-borovsky_middle-game.md §4 C14 (the threat is stronger than its fulfilment)
conditions: The opponent's forcing replies are exhausted or harmless, and the quiet move creates a double threat or an unstoppable plan.
No forcing winning line exists that is simpler.
contrasts: The quiet move gives the defender a tempo for a check that wrecks the idea.
A forcing line wins faster and the quiet move is a showpiece.
A position where every forcing line is already decisive.
contrast_sources: CAP CI-51 (G8: the most effective move, not the prettiest)

soft_prereq_notes.POS.PROPHYLAXIS.D1: a quiet move in a combination often removes a defender's counterplay
soft_prereq_notes.TAC.MATE-SEARCH.D3: the quiet move that leaves the king no defence is searched with the mate-search list

title: Removing the defender

D0.outcome: Explains that a piece defended by one other piece can be won by taking, blocking, pinning or deflecting its only defender first.

D1.outcome: When told 'remove the defender', finds the capture or attack that eliminates the sole defender and wins the target.

D2.outcome: In mixed sets, finds the removal that wins material, and does not play it when the defender's job passes to another piece or the removal costs more than it wins.

D3.outcome: Recounts the square after the removal (recaptures, new defenders, check on recapture) and predicts how adding one defender changes the result.

misconceptions: Capturing the defender always wins the defended piece.
A defender can only be removed by capture.
sources: sources/sheets/edlasker_chess-strategy.md §4 K3 (the count lies: defender capturable by a cheaper piece, forced away, pinned); §7 row K3
sources/sheets/nimzowitsch_my-system.md §4 ideas 21, 27 (destroying a defender; exchange on the pinning square)
conditions: The defender's job is not taken over by another piece after it leaves.
After the removal, the count on the target square favours the attacker, including the recapture sequence.
A defender in the wide sense includes a piece guarding a file entry, an outpost or the castled king.
contrasts: Capturing with the very piece that is holding the king-side together removes your own best defender.
A second defender recaptures, so the removal gains nothing.
The 'defender' captured guards a square that has nothing of value on it.

soft_prereq_notes.TAC.DISCOVER.D2: a discovered attack can remove a defender with tempo

title: Skewers

D0.outcome: Describes a skewer (a line attack on a valuable front piece that must move, exposing a piece behind it) and says how it differs from a pin.

D1.outcome: When told 'find the skewer', finds the check or attack along a line that wins the piece behind.

D2.outcome: In mixed sets with no theme named, finds the skewer when it exists, and does not play it when the front piece can interpose or the rear piece is defended.

D3.outcome: Checks that the skewered piece cannot capture the attacker or give a stronger check first, and counts what the capture of the rear piece nets.

misconceptions: A skewer is just a pin.
A skewer wins the rear piece even when it is defended and cheaper than the attacker.
sources: docs/curriculum-map-v1.md §2 S3 (listed T1-2; no synthesis sheet covers the skewer, so conditions are ours)
sources/sheets/nimzowitsch_my-system.md §4 idea 26 (pin anatomy, for the contrast)
conditions: The front piece is at least as valuable as the rear piece or is the king, so it must move first.
The front piece cannot capture the attacker, interpose, or reply with a check that gains time.
contrasts: The rear piece is defended and worth less than the attacking piece, so the skewer nets only an exchange.
The front piece moves with check, so the rear piece escapes.
The rear piece is worth more than the front piece, which is a pin, and the correct plan is different.

soft_prereq_notes.TAC.PIN.D1: the skewer is the pin reversed, and the two are best taught as a contrast pair

title: Stalemate as a resource

D0.outcome: Explains that a side that is clearly losing can sometimes draw by leaving its opponent a position with no legal move and no check.

D1.outcome: When told 'find the stalemate', finds the move that stalemates, or the sacrifice that forces it.

D2.outcome: In mixed endings, finds the drawing resource for the weaker side and avoids the stalemate when winning, with no theme named.

D3.outcome: Checks the conditions (spare moves, promotion choice, pawn tempo) and predicts how adding a spare pawn move or changing the promoted piece removes the stalemate.

misconceptions: A stalemate is a win for the side that has no move.
Having more material makes a stalemate impossible.
sources: sources/sheets/capablanca_chess-fundamentals.md §4 CI-15, CI-03; §7 row 5 (use the Q v R trap as the first example)
sources/sheets/edlasker_chess-strategy.md §4 K29 (Q v advanced pawn; stalemate as the saving device)
conditions: The defending king has no legal move and is not in check, and no other defending piece can move.
It arises most often with the defender's king on the edge or in a corner.
contrasts: The defender has a spare pawn or piece move, so no stalemate arises.
Promoting to a queen stalemates; promoting to a rook wins (or the reverse), so the choice of piece decides.
A lone king in the middle of the board with room to move.

soft_prereq_notes.FND.PROMOTE.D1: the choice of promoted piece decides many stalemate cases

title: Trapped pieces

D0.outcome: Explains that a piece is trapped when every square it can go to is attacked or occupied and nothing can defend or free it.

D1.outcome: When told 'trap the piece', finds the move that takes away the last escape square.

D2.outcome: In mixed sets, finds the piece that can be won by trapping, and tells a really trapped piece from one that is cut off but can be freed.

D3.outcome: Counts the ways out (capturing a guard, a counter-sacrifice, an interposition) before calling a piece trapped, and sees when the trapped piece can sell itself for a pawn or more.

misconceptions: A piece with no safe move is lost.
A piece shut in behind its own pawns is trapped.
sources: sources/sheets/capablanca_chess-fundamentals.md §4 CI-35 (cutting off a piece from the scene of action); §7 row 38
docs/curriculum-map-v1.1.md §3 (TAC.TRAPPED with POS.OUTOFPLAY as the contrast)
sources/sheets/edlasker_chess-strategy.md §4 K15 (an objective that cannot move away)
conditions: All escape squares are covered and no counter-sacrifice or exchange frees the piece.
The trapping side can attack the piece again before it escapes.
contrasts: A bishop shut in behind its own pawns is out of play, not trapped; a pawn lever frees it at a cost.
The trapped piece captures a guard on the way out and the trap collapses.
A piece with plenty of squares that merely stands badly.

soft_prereq_notes.SAF.LOOSE.D2: the loose piece is the usual target

title: Underpromotion

D0.outcome: Explains why a pawn is sometimes promoted to a knight, rook or bishop instead of a queen.

D1.outcome: When told 'underpromote', finds the promotion that checks or forks, or the one that avoids a stalemate.

D2.outcome: In mixed endings, chooses the right promoted piece and says when the queen is correct.

D3.outcome: Verifies by counting replies that the chosen piece wins or draws where the queen fails, and predicts how moving the enemy king changes the choice.

misconceptions: Promoting to a queen is always at least as good.
sources: sources/sheets/edlasker_chess-strategy.md §4 K29 (queen versus an advanced pawn; stalemate resources)
conditions: A queen would stalemate or lose to a tactic that the other piece avoids, or a knight promotion gives check with a fork.
contrasts: The queen promotion also wins, and the unusual promotion adds nothing.
Promoting to a knight gives an apparent fork that the king escapes.
A pawn that cannot reach the last rank.
note: Tier 4 chosen from the map's T4-5 so that it can follow the stalemate resource; no D4/D5 because underpromotion is too rare in play to evidence. No synthesis sheet covers it; conditions are ours.

title: X-ray and batteries

D0.outcome: Explains that a piece can attack or defend a square 'through' another piece of its own side once the front piece captures or moves.

D1.outcome: When told there is an x-ray, finds the capture sequence in which the rear piece joins in.

D2.outcome: In mixed exchange positions, counts attackers and defenders including the pieces behind others, and finds the winning sequence.

D3.outcome: Predicts how the count changes when a front piece is pinned, removed or exchanged, and verifies the sequence.

misconceptions: Pieces lined up on a file count as one attacker.
sources: sources/sheets/edlasker_chess-strategy.md §4 K3 (a piece's own capture can unmask an attack by another piece, changing the tally); §7 row K3
sources/sheets/nimzowitsch_my-system.md §4 idea 27 (a second rook takes over the file with tempo)
conditions: The rear piece is of the same or a compatible type on the same line and the front piece will leave by capture or move.
The count is taken in cheapest-first order and either side may stop.
contrasts: The front piece cannot capture because it is pinned, so the battery never forms.
The rear piece is worth more than the target, so joining the exchange loses.
A lone piece on the file with nothing behind it.

soft_prereq_notes.POS.OPENFILE.D3: doubling rooks on a file is the usual battery

title: In-between moves

D0.outcome: Explains an in-between move as a forcing move played before the expected recapture or reply.

D1.outcome: When told 'there is an in-between move', finds the check or capture that changes the outcome of an exchange.

D2.outcome: In mixed sets, finds the in-between move in exchange sequences, and does not rely on a recapture that the opponent can sidestep.

D3.outcome: Re-counts an exchange allowing for the opponent's best in-between move; predicts which side gains when a check is available.

misconceptions: After a capture the recapture is automatic.
sources: sources/sheets/edlasker_chess-strategy.md §4 K3 (an own capture can unmask another attack)
conditions: The in-between move creates a threat larger than the recapture and leaves the original capture available.
It is most often a check, because the reply is forced.
contrasts: After the in-between check the target escapes with a tempo, so the original capture is gone.
The in-between move is itself answered by a stronger in-between move.
An exchange with no check or threat available to either side.

soft_prereq_notes.TAC.DOUBLE-CHECK.D1: an in-between check can be a double check

note: No synthesis sheet covers this motif; conditions are ours and must be engine-checked at authoring.
